Dampalo (Varketili, New Jewish Cemetery)

Jewish Cemetery · Tbilisi, Georgia

Not demolished. Tbilisi's Jewish community may trace to the 5th-6th centuries, when Jews reportedly migrated from Mtskheta after Tbilisi became capital; older names for the city, 'Uriatubani' and 'Petkhaini,' echo the Hebrew 'Beth Haim' (house of life, a term for cemetery). A late-9th-century Karaite sect, the 'Tiflisites,' founded by Abu-Imran al-Tiflisi, persisted over 300 years. A 1795 Persian raid burned Tbilisi's synagogues; population grew from 105 (1843) to 4,000 by 1903, with five synagogues active by the early 20th century, peaking at about 20,000 Jews by 1970 before declining sharply to roughly 2,500 today, served by just two active synagogues (the Great Synagogue and Beit Rachel). This is one of three Jewish cemeteries on Tbilisi's outskirts (alongside Navtlughi's Ashkenazi cemetery and the Ortachala cemetery, both now inactive) and is the only one still in use today, serving a mix of Georgian, Ashkenazi, and Mountain Jewish community members. Also called the 'New' Jewish cemetery, it was built in 1950, though its oldest visible tombstone dates only to 1963; its gravestones are notably eclectic and non-traditional, favoring sculpture over engraved text. The site borders a Christian (Armenian) cemetery and continues expanding with newly cleared burial plots.
